newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Quest for new high-yield rice hit by funds crunch.
newsitem.headline: Quest for new high-yield rice hit by funds crunch.

text.p: A tightening of purse strings by major donor countries may slow down research on a new high-yield "super rice", scientists at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) said on Wednesday.
"We may have a $6 million budget shortfall next year which means we have to contract our resources severely. That could jeopardise our research," IRRI director George Rothschild said.
IRRI, the world's premier rice research institute which has been credited with helping eradicate hunger by creating several high-yielding varieties, needs an operating budget of $31 million annually.
Rothschild declined to name the countries that wanted to cut back on grants.

One project in the pipeline that will be affected by the recent budget cut is the development of a variety that has the potential to increase rice yield by 25 percent, or between 12 and 13 tonnes per hectare, Rothschild said.
"It (the budget cut) will affect our efficiency. We will have less people to work with. Our productivity will go down," Gurdev Singh Khush, principal plant breeder of IRRI, told Reuters.
Khush and another IRRI plant scientist, Henry Beachell, were named winners of the $200,000 World Food Prize last month for developing rice varieties that allowed Asia to feed itself.

Beachell developed the "miracle rice" that doubled yields as part of the Green Revolution of 1960s while Khush was responsible for an early maturing, high-yielding variety that is now the most widely planted rice.

IRRI is now perfecting a new breed of thick-stalked "super rice". The new rice variety should be available to farmers in five years, Khush said, after disease resistance is bred into it and its flavour adapted for local tastes.
Rice is the world's number one food and is the staple for nearly 2.5 billion people, or about half the world's population.
In 2025 or 2030, Rotchschild said, there will be over four billion people eating rice.
"This means we have to increase production by 70 percent or more and we have to do this with less land, less water and less labour," he said.
But Rothschild said the budget cuts may force IRRI to cut staff as well as training for rice breeders and agronomists in rice-growing countries.
"I think the rest of the world is so pre-occupied with domestic issues. They don't realise the importance of agriculture to economic development," Rothschild said.
Rothschild appealed to rice-eating countries to help IRRI face the challenge of developing more high-yielding rice varieties to ensure food sufficiency in the next century.
"If you don't support research, how will we be able to (tackle) this challenge of feeding twice as many people in a space of just a generation?" he asked.
The IRRI was formed in 1960 by the Ford and Rockefeller Foundation to promote research in humanity's most vital crop.
More than 30 governments, non profit agencies, and private foundations now support the IRRI.
